docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
PyDataUI is a modern full-stack web framework designed for Data Engineers, Data Analysts, AI/ML Engineers, and Python developers. It bridges the gap between simple toy prototype libraries (Gradio, Streamlit) and complex multi-language web stacks (React + TypeScript + FastAPI).

With PyDataUI: - You write 100% Python. - The backend runs on pyrustapi, an asynchronous HTTP core written in Rust (Tokio & Hyper) delivering lower latency and higher throughput than standard Python servers like Uvicorn. - The UI is styled with Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui design patterns, including full dark mode support. - Reactivity is powered by HTMX server-side rendering (SSR): when state changes, minimal HTML fragments are sent to the browser and swapped into place with zero client JavaScript. - Every state class automatically creates an OpenAPI-documented REST API for data integration.

docs.title: 4. Installation & Requirements
docs.text:
PyDataUI requires Python 3.9+.

# Core framework
pip install pydataui

# With data science & ML dependencies (pandas, plotly, pyarrow)
pip install "pydataui[data]"

# Full installation (data + tunnel + dev)
pip install "pydataui[all]"

docs.title: 5. Quick Start
docs.text:
Create an app file app.py:

from pydataui import App, State
from pydataui.components import Container, Card, Flex, Button, Heading, Divider

class CounterState(State):
    count: int = 0
    def increment(self): self.count += 1
    def decrement(self): self.count -= 1
    def reset(self): self.count = 0

app = App(title="PyDataUI Counter")

@app.page("/")
def home():
    return Container(
        Card(
            title="Reactive Counter",
            children=[
                Flex(
                    Button("-", on_click=CounterState.decrement, variant="danger"),
                    Heading(CounterState.count, level=2),
                    Button("+", on_click=CounterState.increment, variant="success"),
                    align="center", justify="center", gap="lg",
                ),
                Divider(),
                Button("Reset", on_click=CounterState.reset, variant="outline", full_width=True),
            ]
        ),
        max_width="md",
        padding="lg",
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()

Run with the CLI: 

pydataui dev app.py --reload

docs.title: Reactive State & StateVar
docs.text:
State in PyDataUI is defined by subclassing State. Typed class variables become reactive state descriptors:

from pydataui import State

class PipelineState(State):
    batch_size: int = 5000
    is_running: bool = False
    status_log: list = []

    def start_pipeline(self):
        self.is_running = True
        self.status_log.append("Started batch run")

    def stop_pipeline(self):
        self.is_running = False
        self.status_log.append("Halted by operator")
  • When referenced at the class level (e.g. PipelineState.batch_size), it returns a StateVarRef which binds to the current user's session snapshot during rendering.
  • When accessed inside a method (self.batch_size), it operates as a standard Python attribute.

docs.title: Event Handlers & SSR
docs.text:
Buttons, forms, and inputs connect to State methods using props:

# Direct method reference
Button("Start", on_click=PipelineState.start_pipeline)

# Lambda with argument capture
Button("Delete", on_click=lambda id=item.id: TableState.delete_item(id))

# Two-way input binding
Input("Batch Size", bind=PipelineState.batch_size, type="number")

docs.title: Automatic REST APIs
docs.text:
For every registered State, PyDataUI creates endpoints automatically:

Method Endpoint Description GET /api/{State} Full state dictionary serialized to JSON GET /api/{State}/{field} Single field value PUT /api/{State} Update state variables from JSON body DELETE /api/{State} Reset state instance to class defaults POST /api/{State}/{method} Execute a method (accepts optional JSON payload)

Catalog all states and endpoints: 

curl http://localhost:8000/api

Interactive Swagger UI: - http://localhost:8000/docs - http://localhost:8000/api/docs

    ShadCard, ShadCardHeader, ShadCardTitle, ShadCardContent,

docs.title: 10. Port Forwarding (share=True)
docs.text:
Share your application with remote stakeholders, clients, or team members with a single flag:

app.run(share=True)
Or via CLI: 
pydataui run app.py --share

Tunnels use pyngrok if installed, or fallback to encrypted SSH port-forwarding via serveo.net.

docs.title: class App(title="PyDataUI App", description="", version="0.3.3", debug=False, **kwargs)
docs.text:
The central application object integrating routing, state snapshots, REST APIs, and the HTTP server.

Request bodies are capped by max_request_size (default 10 * 1024 * 1024 bytes). Oversized bodies are rejected with HTTP 413 before routing; requests that declare an oversized Content-Length are rejected without being read.

docs.title: Methods:
docs.text:
• app.page(path: str, title: Optional[str] = None, layout: Optional[Callable] = None) Decorator registering an SSR page route. The decorated function must return a Component or HTML string.
  • app.api(path: str, method: str = 'GET', public=False, roles=(), **kwargs) Decorator registering a custom JSON endpoint on the underlying pyrustapi engine.
  • app.setup_auth(auth_manager: AuthManager, allow_registration=False) Mounts /api/auth/* endpoints and registers authentication middleware handlers.
  • app.run(host=None, port=None, reload=False, workers=1, share=False, auth=None) Starts the HTTP server.
  • share=True: Launches a public internet tunnel (port forwarding) and prints the public URL.
  • workers=N: Number of pyrustapi multi-threaded worker processes.

docs.title: Properties:
docs.text:
• app.title: Application title.
  • app.routes: Mapping of registered page routes to handler functions.
  • app.api_routes: Mapping of registered custom API routes.

docs.title: class State
docs.text:
Base class for reactive application state stores. - Annotated class variables become reactive StateVar descriptors. - Methods serve as event handlers and automatic REST actions.

class MyState(State):
    count: int = 0
    def increment(self): self.count += 1
  • Class-level access (MyState.count): Returns a StateVarRef proxy that evaluates against the active session snapshot during rendering.
  • Instance-level access (self.count): Standard Python value.
  • to_dict() -> Dict[str, Any]: Serializes the current state instance to a JSON-compatible dictionary.
  • reset(): Resets all state variables back to class default values.

docs.title: class AuthManager(secret_key: str, token_expire_hours: int = 24)
docs.text: Handles user authentication, password hashing (pbkdf2_hmac), JWT encoding/decoding, and API key management.

docs.title: Methods:
docs.text:
• add_user(username: str, password: str, email: str = "", roles: List[str] = None) -> User Creates a user with hashed password. Raises ValueError if username exists.
  • authenticate(username: str, password: str) -> Optional[str] Verifies credentials and returns a signed JWT token, or None.
  • verify_token(token: str) -> Optional[User] Decodes JWT token and returns the User object if valid.
  • create_api_key(name: str, user_id: str, scopes: List[str] = None, expires_days: Optional[int] = None) -> APIKey Generates a production API key starting with pdu_live_.
  • verify_api_key(key: str) -> Optional[APIKey] Validates API key token, increments usage_count, updates last_used.
  • revoke_api_key(key_id: str) Deactivates an API key.
  • list_api_keys(user_id: str) -> List[APIKey] Returns all active API keys for a user.
  • require_auth_middleware(request) -> Optional[User] Extracts and verifies user from Authorization: Bearer <token> or pdu-auth cookie.

docs.title: Authentication, Authorization & API Keys Guide
docs.text: PyDataUI provides a built-in enterprise authentication system designed for data platforms, analytics portals, and automated ETL pipelines.

docs.title: 1. Core Architecture
docs.text: PyDataUI's auth module (pydataui.auth) supports: - Session & JWT Authentication: Sign in via web form or REST API to obtain signed JWT tokens. - Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Assign roles to users and enforce role permissions on pages and endpoints. - Production API Keys (pdu_live_...): Generate scoped API keys for Airflow, Prefect, Cron jobs, and external data consumers. - Zero Heavy Dependencies: Uses standard library hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac for password hashing and PyJWT for JWT signing.

docs.title: 2. Setup & Configuration
docs.text:
from pydataui import App
from pydataui.auth import AuthManager, Role

app = App(title="Corporate Analytics")
auth = AuthManager(
    secret_key="your-secure-random-secret-key-min-32-chars!",
    token_expire_hours=24
)

# Seed initial users
admin = auth.add_user(
    username="admin",
    password="SuperSecurePassword123!",
    email="admin@company.com",
    roles=[Role.ADMIN, Role.DATA_ENGINEER]
)

analyst = auth.add_user(
    username="jane",
    password="JanePassword456!",
    email="jane@company.com",
    roles=[Role.DATA_ANALYST]
)

# Attach auth routes and handlers to app
app.setup_auth(auth)

Calling app.setup_auth(auth) automatically mounts the following REST endpoints: - POST /api/auth/login → Authenticates credentials, returns { "token": "<jwt>" } - POST /api/auth/logout → Invalidate session - GET /api/auth/me → Returns user profile and assigned roles - POST /api/auth/register → Register new user account - GET /api/auth/keys → List user's active API keys - POST /api/auth/keys → Generate a new API key - DELETE /api/auth/keys/{key_id} → Revoke an API key

docs.title: APIKeyManager
docs.text:
Provides a complete UI for listing keys, generating new keys, and revoking keys: 

from pydataui.auth import APIKeyManager

@app.page("/settings/keys")
def keys_page():
    user = auth.require_auth_middleware(request)
    keys = auth.list_api_keys(user.id) if user else []
    return Container(
        APIKeyManager(keys=keys)
    )

docs.title: ⚡ Performance Benchmarks: PyDataUI (PyRustAPI) vs FastAPI (Uvicorn)
docs.text:
This benchmark suite provides a rigorous, head-to-head comparison between PyDataUI (powered by the Rust pyrustapi engine on Tokio/Hyper) and FastAPI (running on uvicorn with uvloop).

All tests measure real HTTP performance over loopback TCP sockets using ApacheBench (ab), evaluating both Real GET (payload serialization) and Real POST (Pydantic model validation and serialization) on a local development machine.

docs.title: Profile A: High-Concurrency Stress Test (c=100, 5,000 requests)
docs.text:
Under extreme concurrency (100 concurrent workers), PyDataUI demonstrates resilience and stability, while FastAPI/Uvicorn suffers severe queuing contention on asynchronous POST:

Benchmark Workload PyDataUI (pyrustapi) FastAPI (uvicorn + uvloop) Speedup Advantage PyDataUI Latency (Mean) FastAPI Latency (Mean) Real POST (Async Pydantic) 1,172.9 req/s 220.3 req/s ⚡ 5.32x Faster 85.26 ms 453.85 ms (p99: 17.6s) Real GET (Sync) 4,066.8 req/s 1,679.0 req/s ⚡ 2.42x Faster 24.59 ms 59.56 ms Real POST (Sync Pydantic) 1,845.0 req/s 935.3 req/s ⚡ 1.97x Faster 54.20 ms 106.92 ms Real GET (Async I/O) 2,444.8 req/s 1,557.6 req/s ⚡ 1.57x Faster 40.90 ms 64.20 ms

docs.text:

docs.title: 🏗️ Why is PyDataUI Faster?
docs.text:
1. Compiled Rust Core Engine (pyrustapi):
  2. HTTP parsing, TCP socket management, keep-alive framing, and header processing are handled in compiled Rust using Tokio and Hyper.

  3. Python only executes the application logic and handler body, eliminating Python interpreter overhead for low-level HTTP protocol handling.

  4. Optimized Multi-Threaded Dispatching:

  5. Tokio distributes incoming requests across native OS threads before bridging into Python, maximizing CPU core utilization.

  6. Zero-Overhead Memory Shuttling:

  7. Request payloads and headers are mapped directly from Rust memory into Python objects via PyO3 without redundant intermediate string copying.

docs.title: CSS Reference for Developers
docs.text:
PyDataUI ships a small, dependency-free CSS layer for its core components and uses Tailwind CSS for utility styling and shadcn/ui tokens. This guide documents that layer for developers who are theming an application, writing custom components, or changing the framework stylesheet.

The stylesheet is a single plain-CSS file:

pydataui/styling/css/pydataui.css

There is no Sass, PostCSS, CSS-in-JS, or build step for this file. It is served unchanged at /_pdu/static/pydataui.css.

For semantic HTML APIs and generated markup, see the HTML Reference. For task-oriented examples, see UI Customization & Tailwind.

docs.title: 1. Stylesheet Architecture
docs.text:
The stylesheet is organized into numbered sections:

Section Contents 1 Reset and base element styles 2 --pdu-* design tokens and dark overrides 3 Layout: containers, flex, grid, stacks, cards, dividers 4 Typography 5 Forms and controls 6 Data display: tables, lists, badges, stats, avatars 7 Feedback: alerts, progress, spinners, skeletons, toasts 8 Navigation: navbar, sidebar, tabs, breadcrumbs, pagination 9 Overlays: modals, drawers, popovers, dropdowns 10 Media and icons 11 Animations and keyframes 12 Utility classes and responsive visibility

The layer follows three rules:

  1. Framework selectors use the pdu- prefix.
  2. Values that participate in theming come from CSS custom properties; structural values such as fixed icon sizes may remain local.
  3. Application-specific styling should use class_name or the --pdu-* tokens, not edits to framework selectors.

docs.title: Load Order
docs.text:
For a normal application page, styles are applied in this order:

Tailwind Play CDN
  -> generated shadcn CSS variables
  -> App(custom_css=...)
  -> pydataui.css
  -> App(stylesheets=[...])
  -> App(head=...)

Consequences:

  • custom_css is emitted before pydataui.css. If both rules have equal specificity, the framework rule wins.
  • External stylesheets passed to App(stylesheets=[...]) load after the framework and are the cleanest place for application overrides.
  • Inline styles passed through style={...} override both, except for !important declarations.
  • Tailwind utilities and pdu-* classes generally have equal single-class specificity. Avoid relying on source order when they conflict; use a more specific selector, an arbitrary value, or ! on the Tailwind utility.

docs.title: 2. Naming Conventions
docs.text:
Pattern Meaning Example pdu Base class added to every component <h1 class="pdu"> pdu-<block> Block or component .pdu-card, .pdu-alert pdu-<block>-<part> Part of a block .pdu-card-header, .pdu-modal-body pdu-<block>-<modifier> Variant or state .pdu-btn-primary, .pdu-tab-active pdu-<property>-<value> Utility .pdu-mt-md, .pdu-text-sm, .pdu-hidden

Names are flat, not BEM-style. Modifiers are separate classes, not descendant selectors, so an element can combine them:

<button class="pdu pdu-btn pdu-btn-primary pdu-btn-lg">Run pipeline</button>

Do not use pdu-* names for application-only classes. Prefix custom classes with your product or use Tailwind utilities. This avoids collisions during framework upgrades.

docs.title: Overriding Tokens
docs.text:
Use App(custom_css=...) for application-wide token changes:

from pydataui import App

app = App(
    title="Operations Portal",
    custom_css="""
    :root {
      --pdu-color-primary: #0f766e;
      --pdu-color-primary-hover: #115e59;
      --pdu-color-primary-light: #ccfbf1;
      --pdu-radius-lg: 0.75rem;
    }
    """,
)

Token overrides inherit everywhere the token is referenced. Prefer this over copying and editing component rules.

docs.title: 4. Theme Layers and Dark Mode
docs.text:
PyDataUI has two related token layers:

Layer Variables Consumed by Framework layer --pdu-* Native pdu-* component classes and pydataui.html tags shadcn/Tailwind layer --background, --foreground, --primary, --card, --muted, --border, etc. shadcn components and Tailwind color utilities such as bg-card, text-muted-foreground

App(theme=...) controls the shadcn/Tailwind layer:

App(theme="light")  # no dark class
App(theme="dark")   # class="dark" on <html>
App(theme="auto")   # adds class="dark" when the OS prefers dark mode

App(palette=...) selects the shadcn token values. Available palettes are zinc, slate, blue, violet, green, rose, orange, and emerald.

The framework layer activates its dark token block through either .dark or [data-theme="dark"]. This means native pdu-* components follow App(theme="dark") as well:

[data-theme='dark'], .dark {
  --pdu-color-bg: #111827;
  --pdu-color-bg-secondary: #1f2937;
  --pdu-color-text: #f9fafb;
  --pdu-color-border: #374151;
  /* additional dark values */
}

To override framework dark values, put the override under the same selector:

custom_css="""
.dark {
  --pdu-color-primary: #2dd4bf;
  --pdu-color-primary-light: #134e4a;
}
"""

Because custom_css is loaded before pydataui.css, an equal-specificity .dark rule would be overwritten by the framework's dark block. Use a more specific selector or a stylesheet that loads after the framework:

html.dark {
  --pdu-color-primary: #2dd4bf;
}

docs.text:
The Tailwind configuration maps these utility colors to CSS variables:

Tailwind utility family CSS variables bg-background, text-foreground --background, --foreground bg-card, text-card-foreground --card, --card-foreground bg-primary, text-primary-foreground --primary, --primary-foreground bg-secondary, text-secondary-foreground --secondary, --secondary-foreground bg-muted, text-muted-foreground --muted, --muted-foreground bg-accent, text-accent-foreground --accent, --accent-foreground bg-destructive, text-destructive-foreground --destructive, --destructive-foreground border-border, border-input, ring-ring --border, --input, --ring

The shadcn values are HSL channel triplets, for example --primary: 240 5.9% 10%. They are consumed through hsl(var(--primary)), so overrides must use the same format.

docs.title: 12. Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui Integration
docs.text:
Every component accepts class_name, which is appended after its framework classes:

from pydataui.html import Section, H2, P

Section(
    H2("Pipeline health", class_name="text-2xl font-semibold tracking-tight"),
    P("Updated two minutes ago", class_name="text-sm text-muted-foreground"),
    class_name="pdu-p-lg max-w-3xl mx-auto bg-card border border-border rounded-xl",
)

Use the layers for different jobs:

Need Use Standard component appearance Native component or pdu-* class Application spacing, layout, responsive behavior Tailwind utilities in class_name Brand colors and dark-mode colors App(palette=...), tailwind_config, or shadcn token overrides Framework primitive colors --pdu-* token overrides Reusable project component Subclass Component and return pdu-* plus project classes

docs.title: Custom Tailwind Theme Values
docs.text:
App(tailwind_config={...}) deep-merges into the default Tailwind theme used by the Play CDN:

app = App(
    tailwind_config={
        "theme": {
            "extend": {
                "colors": {
                    "brand": "#0ea5e9",
                },
                "fontFamily": {
                    "mono": ["Fira Code", "monospace"],
                },
            }
        }
    }
)

After this, text-brand and font-mono are available in class_name values.

docs.title: shadcn Component Styles
docs.text: The shadcn components are styled with Tailwind classes and the shadcn token layer, not with pdu-* classes. They follow App(theme=...) and App(palette=...) directly. To style them consistently with native components, align both token layers rather than overriding individual shadcn component classes.

docs.title: Adding a New Framework Primitive
docs.text:
1. Add a token to :root if the value should be themeable.
  2. Add a .pdu-* rule in the appropriate numbered section of pydataui.css.
  3. Reference existing tokens with var(--pdu-...) rather than repeating literal values.
  4. Add a modifier class for each variant instead of writing one-off selectors in application code.
  5. Test in light and dark mode, at mobile and desktop widths, and with keyboard focus.
  6. Update this reference if you add a public class.

Example:

.pdu-run-state {
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: var(--pdu-spacing-xs);
  padding: var(--pdu-spacing-xs) var(--pdu-spacing-sm);
  border-radius: var(--pdu-radius-full);
  background-color: var(--pdu-color-bg-secondary);
  color: var(--pdu-color-text-secondary);
  font-size: var(--pdu-font-size-xs);
  font-weight: 600;
}

.pdu-run-state-success {
  background-color: var(--pdu-color-success-light);
  color: var(--pdu-color-success-hover);
}

docs.title: Adding a Custom Component
docs.text:
Prefer composing existing classes:

from pydataui import Component

class RunState(Component):
    tag = "span"

    def __init__(self, label, state="success", **kwargs):
        super().__init__(label, **kwargs)
        self.state = state

    def _get_classes(self):
        return super()._get_classes() + [
            "pdu-run-state",
            f"pdu-run-state-{self.state}",
        ]

If the component is reusable beyond one application, add the corresponding styles to the framework stylesheet and cover them with a rendering test. If it is application-specific, keep the CSS in custom_css or a stylesheet passed through App(stylesheets=[...]).

docs.title: Override Strategy
docs.text:
Choose the least invasive option that works:

Need Preferred approach One instance class_name with Tailwind utilities or an inline style One application custom_css with a scoped selector or tokens Shared across applications Framework token override or new reusable component Framework bug or missing primitive Change pydataui.css and add tests

Avoid targeting generated IDs such as #pdu-a1b2c3d4. IDs are instance-specific and are not a stable styling contract. Use classes, semantic elements, or explicit id values that you control.

docs.title: 14. Testing CSS Changes
docs.text:
CSS changes should be verified at three levels:

# Unit tests for rendering and class contracts
python -m pytest -q --ignore=tests/test_browser_security.py

# Browser tests with a real browser and stylesheet
PYDATAUI_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE="/Applications/ego lite.app/Contents/MacOS/ego lite" \
PYDATAUI_REQUIRE_BROWSER=1 \
PYDATAUI_REQUIRE_REAL_STYLES=1 \
python -m pytest tests/test_browser_security.py -q

# Documentation build
python -m mkdocs build --strict

For a manual check:

  1. Render a page in light and dark mode.
  2. Resize to mobile, tablet, and desktop widths.
  3. Confirm text and focus rings meet contrast expectations.
  4. Check that components still work when Tailwind's CDN is unavailable; core pdu-* styles should remain usable.
  5. Inspect the computed value of the relevant --pdu-* token.

docs.title: UI Customization Guide: Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui & HTML
docs.text:
PyDataUI gives you complete design freedom. Whether you prefer utility-first styling with Tailwind CSS, pre-built shadcn/ui components, semantic HTML tags in pure Python, or direct raw HTML/SVG templates, you can build any interface without feeling boxed into rigid defaults.

Developer references

For the full tag and attribute contract, see the HTML Reference. For framework tokens, class names, dark mode, and cascade rules, see the CSS Reference.

docs.title: 1. Quick Overview
docs.text: Customization Layer How to Use Example Tailwind CSS Pass class_name="..." to any component Box(class_name="p-6 bg-slate-900 rounded-2xl shadow-xl hover:scale-105 transition-all") shadcn/ui Components Import ShadCard, ShadButton, ShadDialog, etc. ShadButton("Save", variant="default", size="lg") Theme Palettes Set palette="..." on App() App(theme="dark", palette="violet") Semantic HTML in Python Import from pydataui.html from pydataui.html import Section, Header, Nav, Svg, Path, H1, P Raw HTML & SVG Use Html("""<svg>...</svg>""") Html('<div class="badge">Live</div>') Custom Tailwind Config Pass tailwind_config={...} to App() App(tailwind_config={"theme": {"extend": {"colors": {"brand": "#ff5722"}}}}) External Styles & Scripts Pass stylesheets and scripts to App() App(stylesheets=["https://fonts.googleapis.com/..."])

docs.title: 2. Tailwind CSS Styling
docs.text: Tailwind CSS Play CDN is loaded by default. Every component accepts the class_name parameter.

docs.title: Responsive Breakpoints & Flex/Grid
docs.text:
from pydataui import Component, Text
from pydataui.html import Div

grid_layout = Div(
    Div(Text("Sidebar"), class_name="w-full md:w-64 bg-slate-100 p-4 rounded-xl"),
    Div(Text("Main Content"), class_name="flex-1 bg-white p-6 rounded-xl shadow-sm"),
    class_name="flex flex-col md:flex-row gap-6 p-6 max-w-7xl mx-auto"
)

)

from pydataui.components.shadcn import ShadButton

btn = ShadButton(
    "Explore Models",
    class_name="bg-gradient-to-r from-violet-600 to-indigo-600 hover:from-violet-700 hover:to-indigo-700 text-white font-semibold px-6 py-3 rounded-xl shadow-lg hover:shadow-violet-500/25 active:scale-95 transition-all duration-200"

docs.title: 3. shadcn/ui Theme Palettes & Components
docs.text: PyDataUI comes with built-in support for shadcn/ui color palettes and design tokens.

docs.title: Selecting a Theme Palette
docs.text:
Choose a palette when initializing your App: 

from pydataui import App

app = App(
    title="Data Studio",
    theme="dark",      # Options: 'light', 'dark', 'auto' (detects system dark mode)
    palette="violet"   # Options: 'zinc', 'slate', 'blue', 'violet', 'green', 'rose', 'orange'
)

Each palette automatically configures CSS variables for :root and .dark: - --primary & --primary-foreground - --secondary & --secondary-foreground - --card & --card-foreground - --muted & --muted-foreground - --accent & --accent-foreground - --destructive & --destructive-foreground - --border, --input, --ring, --radius

docs.title: Built-In shadcn/ui Components
docs.text: All shadcn components can be imported from pydataui.components.shadcn or pydataui.components:

docs.title: Buttons
docs.text:
from pydataui.components.shadcn import ShadButton

ShadButton("Primary Button", variant="default")
ShadButton("Destructive Action", variant="destructive")
ShadButton("Outline Option", variant="outline")
ShadButton("Secondary", variant="secondary")
ShadButton("Ghost", variant="ghost")
ShadButton("Link Style", variant="link")
Supported sizes: size="default", size="sm", size="lg", size="icon".

docs.title: Cards
docs.text:
from pydataui.components.shadcn import (
    ShadCard, ShadCardHeader, ShadCardTitle, ShadCardDescription,
    ShadCardContent, ShadCardFooter, ShadButton
)

card = ShadCard(
    ShadCardHeader(
        ShadCardTitle("Model Deployment"),
        ShadCardDescription("Manage endpoint scaling and compute clusters.")
    ),
    ShadCardContent(
        Text("Current status: Healthy across 3 replicas.")
    ),
    ShadCardFooter(
        ShadButton("Scale Up", variant="default")
    ),
    class_name="max-w-md shadow-md"
)

docs.title: Modals & Drawers (Dialog & Sheet)
docs.text:
Driven by pure Python state without writing JavaScript: 

from pydataui import State
from pydataui.components.shadcn import ShadDialog, ShadSheet, ShadButton

class ModalState(State):
    is_open: bool = False

    def open_modal(self):
        self.is_open = True

    def close_modal(self):
        self.is_open = False

dialog = ShadDialog(
    Text("Do you want to delete this dataset? This action cannot be undone."),
    title="Confirm Action",
    description="Permanent deletion warning",
    open=ModalState.is_open,
    on_close=ModalState.close_modal
)

docs.title: Inputs, Selects, Switches, & Forms
docs.text:
from pydataui.components.shadcn import (
    ShadInput, ShadTextarea, ShadSelect, ShadCheckbox, ShadSwitch, ShadBadge
)

ShadInput(bind=FormState.search_query, placeholder="Search tables...")
ShadSelect(options=["PostgreSQL", "BigQuery", "Snowflake"], bind=FormState.db_type)
ShadSwitch(checked=FormState.enable_cache, label="Enable Query Cache")
ShadBadge("Production", variant="default")

docs.title: 4. Semantic HTML in Pure Python (pydataui.html)
docs.text:
Instead of being restricted to high-level widgets, you can compose standard semantic HTML tags directly in Python using pydataui.html:

from pydataui.html import (
    Header, Nav, Main, Section, Footer, Article, Aside,
    Div, Span, P, H1, H2, H3, H4, A, Ul, Li,
    Svg, Path, Circle, Rect
)

page_layout = Section(
    Header(
        Nav(
            Span("My Brand", class_name="font-extrabold text-xl"),
            A("Documentation", href="/docs", class_name="text-sm hover:underline"),
            class_name="flex justify-between items-center max-w-7xl mx-auto p-4"
        ),
        class_name="border-b bg-card/80 backdrop-blur-md"
    ),
    Main(
        H1("Semantic HTML in Python", class_name="text-3xl font-bold tracking-tight"),
        P("Write native tags with Tailwind classes and Python reactivity.", class_name="text-muted-foreground mt-2"),
        class_name="p-8 max-w-7xl mx-auto"
    ),
    Footer(
        P("© 2026 PyDataUI", class_name="text-center text-xs text-muted-foreground"),
        class_name="border-t p-4"
    ),
    class_name="min-h-screen bg-background"
)

docs.title: SVG Icons & Vector Graphics
docs.text:
Create clean vector icons without external asset bundles: 

from pydataui.html import Svg, Path

bolt_icon = Svg(
    Path(d="M13 10V3L4 14h7v7l9-11h-7z"),
    viewBox="0 0 24 24",
    fill="currentColor",
    class_name="w-6 h-6 text-amber-500"
)

docs.title: HTML5 Boolean Attributes
docs.text: PyDataUI intelligently formats HTML boolean attributes according to HTML5 standards: - disabled=True renders as disabled - disabled=False is completely omitted (no invalid disabled="False") - required=True, checked=True, readonly=True, autofocus=True work out of the box.

docs.title: 5. Raw HTML & Custom Templates (Html / RawHtml)
docs.text:
If you have existing HTML snippets, complex SVG graphics, or third-party web embeds, use Html:

from pydataui import Html

custom_embed = Html("""
<div class="relative overflow-hidden rounded-2xl bg-slate-900 p-8 text-white shadow-2xl">
    <div class="absolute -right-10 -top-10 h-40 w-40 rounded-full bg-violet-600/30 blur-3xl"></div>
    <h3 class="text-xl font-bold">Hardware Accelerated Streaming</h3>
    <p class="text-slate-400 text-sm mt-2">Zero JavaScript required on the client side.</p>
</div>
""")

docs.title: 6. Application-Level Customization (App Configuration)
docs.text:
Customize fonts, third-party libraries, and Tailwind themes directly when creating the App:

from pydataui import App

app = App(
    title="Analytics Portal",
    theme="dark",          # 'light', 'dark', or 'auto'
    palette="blue",        # 'zinc', 'slate', 'blue', 'violet', 'green', 'rose', 'orange'

    # Custom Tailwind extensions
    tailwind_config={
        "theme": {
            "extend": {
                "colors": {
                    "brand": "#0ea5e9",
                    "accent-glow": "#38bdf8"
                },
                "fontFamily": {
                    "mono": ["Fira Code", "monospace"]
                }
            }
        }
    },

    # Custom Google Fonts or external CSS
    stylesheets=[
        "https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Fira+Code:wght@400;600&display=swap"
    ],

    # External JavaScript CDN libraries (e.g. Canvas Confetti, Lucide)
    scripts=[
        "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/canvas-confetti@1.9.3/dist/confetti.browser.min.js"
    ],

    # Custom global CSS rules
    custom_css="""
    body { font-family: 'Inter', sans-serif; }
    code, pre { font-family: 'Fira Code', monospace; }
    """,

    # Custom <head> tags (e.g. meta tags, OpenGraph, favicon)
    head="""
    <meta name="description" content="Production Analytics Portal powered by PyDataUI">
    <link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="data:image/svg+xml,<svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' viewBox='0 0 100 100'><text y='.9em' font-size='90'>🚀</text></svg>">
    """
)

docs.title: 7. Creating Reusable Custom Components
docs.text:
You can encapsulate your own custom UI design system components by subclassing Component:

from pydataui import Component

class GlassCard(Component):
    """Reusable Glassmorphism Card with Tailwind CSS."""
    tag = "div"

    def _get_classes(self):
        return [
            "backdrop-blur-xl bg-card/60 border border-border/50",
            "rounded-2xl p-6 shadow-xl hover:shadow-2xl transition-all duration-300"
        ]

# Usage:
card = GlassCard(
    H2("Custom Glass Component", class_name="text-lg font-bold"),
    P("Encapsulated styling that can be reused across pages.")
)

docs.title: 8. Working Example
docs.text:
See the full working showcase in examples/custom_ui_app.py:

python examples/custom_ui_app.py
Open http://127.0.0.1:8080 to inspect the dark theme, violet palette, interactive progress bars, and custom SVG animations.

docs.title: Data Science & Engineering Components Guide
docs.text:
PyDataUI provides first-class native components built specifically for data professionals. Rather than wiring together complex frontend widgets, you can pass Python data structures, pandas DataFrames, and Plotly charts directly to PyDataUI components.

For complete page layouts, see Data Team Page Templates, which compose these components into analyst, data-quality, pipeline-operations, and ML-registry pages.

docs.title: DataFrameTable
docs.text:
Renders a pandas DataFrame as a scrollable, styled table with shadcn design patterns.

from pydataui.components.data_science import DataFrameTable
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("sales_data.csv")

# Render top 50 rows
DataFrameTable(df=df, max_rows=50)

Props: - df: pandas.DataFrame instance. - max_rows: Maximum rows to render (default: 100).

docs.title: PlotlyChart
docs.text:
Embeds interactive Plotly charts with auto-resizing and responsive layouts.

from pydataui.components.data_science import PlotlyChart
import plotly.express as px

fig = px.bar(
    df, x="quarter", y="revenue", color="region",
    title="Quarterly Regional Revenue",
    barmode="group"
)

PlotlyChart(figure=fig, height=450)

Props: - figure: Plotly Figure instance. - height: Pixel height of the rendered chart (default: 400).

docs.title: MetricCard
docs.text:
Displays key business performance indicators (KPIs) with value formatting, delta indicators, and icons.

from pydataui.components.data_science import MetricCard

MetricCard(
    title="Monthly Active Users",
    value=284500,
    format=",.0f",             # Formats as "284,500"
    delta="+12.4% vs last mo",
    delta_type="increase",      # 'increase' (green) | 'decrease' (red) | 'neutral'
    icon="👥",
    description="Calculated based on unique 30-day token events"
)

docs.text:
Grid of cards summarizing model evaluation metrics.

from pydataui.components.data_science import ModelMetrics

ModelMetrics(

docs.title: PipelineStatus
docs.text:
Real-time step tracker for ETL/ELT pipelines, Spark jobs, and DAGs.

from pydataui.components.data_science import PipelineStatus

PipelineStatus(
    steps=[
        {"name": "1. Extract from S3 Buckets", "status": "success", "message": "2.4GB in 12s"},
        {"name": "2. Data Cleansing & Validation", "status": "success", "message": "0 schema violations"},
        {"name": "3. PySpark Aggregations", "status": "running", "message": "Stage 4 of 8 active"},
        {"name": "4. Load to ClickHouse Data Mart", "status": "pending", "message": "Awaiting stage 3"},
        {"name": "5. Refresh Metabase Dashboards", "status": "pending", "message": "Awaiting stage 4"},
    ]
)
Status types: 'success' (green), 'running' (animated blue pulse), 'pending' (gray), 'failed' (red), 'skipped' (yellow).

docs.title: SQLEditor
docs.text:
SQL query console with query parameter binding and an inline Run action button.

from pydataui.components.data_science import SQLEditor
from pydataui import State

class QueryState(State):
    query_text: str = "SELECT * FROM transactions LIMIT 100;"

    def run_query(self):
        # Execute query against database
        ...

SQLEditor(
    bind=QueryState.query_text,
    on_run=QueryState.run_query,
    rows=10,
    placeholder="Enter your SQL query here..."
)

docs.title: FileDownload & DataUpload
docs.text:
In-browser data interchange components.

from pydataui.components.data_science import FileDownload, DataUpload

# Export CSV button
FileDownload(
    filename="aggregated_report.csv",
    content="date,metric\n2024-01-01,100\n",
    label="Download CSV Export"
)

DataUpload(
    accept=".csv,.parquet,.json",
    on_upload="/api/data/upload"
)

docs.text:
Pretty-printed technical data displays.

from pydataui.components.data_science import JSONViewer, CodeBlock

# Collapsible formatted JSON
JSONViewer(
    data={"model": "Llama-3-70B", "quantization": "4-bit", "context_window": 8192}

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName('Ingest').getOrCreate()
df = spark.read.parquet('s3://lake/raw/*')
""",
    language="python"

docs.title: Data Team Page Templates
docs.text:
PyDataUI ships four low-code page templates for common data-team workflows. Each template returns a normal Container component, so it works with server-rendered pages, state-driven actions, mounting, and authentication exactly like any other component tree.

Visual examples: Open the generated template gallery to see all four pages rendered in a standalone HTML page.

from pydataui import App
from pydataui.templates import analyst_dashboard

app = App(title="Analytics")

@app.page("/")
def home():
    return analyst_dashboard(
        metrics={"Revenue": "$48,250", "Orders": "1,284"},
    )

Templates are available from both pydataui.templates and the root package:

from pydataui import templates
from pydataui.templates import (
    analyst_dashboard,
    data_quality_dashboard,
    pipeline_operations,
    model_registry,
)

docs.title: Choosing a template
docs.text: Role Template Typical content Data analyst analyst_dashboard KPIs, trend chart, filters, records, CSV export Analytics engineer data_quality_dashboard Quality score, dataset catalog, schema checks, uploads Data engineer pipeline_operations Pipeline steps, inventory, activity timeline, run history ML engineer model_registry Model metrics, confusion matrix, feature importance, versions

docs.title: Shared behavior
docs.text:
• metrics accepts a mapping of label to value, or a list of dictionaries with title, value, delta, delta_type, icon, and description keys.
  • Tables accept a list of row dictionaries/lists, a component such as Table, or a pandas DataFrame (rendered through DataFrameTable).
  • Status-like columns (status, state, health, severity, stage) are rendered as colored badges.
  • Strings from application data are escaped by the underlying components.
  • Every template accepts actions=[...] for header buttons or links.
  • Aliases are available: quality_dashboard, pipeline_dashboard, and ml_registry.

docs.title: Analyst dashboard
docs.text:
analyst_dashboard(*, title, subtitle, metrics, filters, chart, chart_title, table, table_columns, table_title, export, actions)

    metrics={"Revenue": "$48,250", "Orders": "1,284", "Conversion": "4.8%"},
    filters=[Input("Region", placeholder="All regions")],

    table=[
        {"Region": "North", "Revenue": "$12,400"},
        {"Region": "South", "Revenue": "$9,850"},
    ],
    export=FileDownload(
        filename="revenue.csv",
        content="region,revenue\nNorth,12400\n",
        label="Export CSV",
        mime_type="text/csv",
    ),
)

docs.title: Analysts: pandas, Plotly, and an export
docs.text:
Templates accept a pandas DataFrame directly for the table and any component for chart slots. PlotlyChart is used here when Plotly is installed.

import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px

from pydataui import App
from pydataui.components import FileDownload
from pydataui.components.data_science import PlotlyChart
from pydataui.templates import analyst_dashboard

app = App(title="Monthly Revenue")

@app.page("/")
def revenue():
    frame = pd.DataFrame(
        [
            {"month": "Jul", "region": "North", "revenue": 12400},
            {"month": "Aug", "region": "North", "revenue": 13800},
            {"month": "Sep", "region": "North", "revenue": 15100},
        ]
    )

    return analyst_dashboard(
        metrics={
            "Rows": len(frame),
            "Revenue": f"${frame['revenue'].sum():,.0f}",
        },
        chart=PlotlyChart(px.bar(frame, x="month", y="revenue")),
        table=frame,
        export=FileDownload(
            filename="revenue.csv",
            content=frame.to_csv(index=False),
            label="Download data",
            mime_type="text/csv",
        ),
    )

docs.title: Data engineers: refresh a pipeline from state
docs.text:
Templates resolve State references each render, so action handlers can update the displayed runs and metrics without bespoke frontend code.

from pydataui import App, State
from pydataui.components import Button
from pydataui.templates import pipeline_operations

class PipelineState(State):
    runs = [
        {"Run": "run_1042", "Duration": "8m 12s", "Status": "success"},
        {"Run": "run_1041", "Duration": "0m 41s", "Status": "failed"},
    ]

    def trigger(self):
        next_run = f"run_{len(self.runs) + 1041}"
        self.runs = [
            {"Run": next_run, "Duration": "running", "Status": "running"},
            *self.runs[:2],
        ]

app = App(title="Pipeline Console")

@app.page("/")
def pipelines():
    return pipeline_operations(
        metrics={"Tracked runs": len(PipelineState.runs)},
        pipeline={
            "name": "warehouse_daily",
            "status": "running",
            "steps": [
                {"name": "Extract Postgres", "status": "success"},
                {"name": "Transform with dbt", "status": "running"},
            ],
        },
        runs=PipelineState.runs,
        actions=[
            Button("Trigger run", on_click=PipelineState.trigger),
        ],
    )

docs.title: Analytics engineers: receive an uploaded file
docs.text:
DataUpload accepts either a URL or a State method. The template handles the layout; your handler validates and stores the file.

from pydataui import App, State
from pydataui.components import DataUpload
from pydataui.templates import data_quality_dashboard

class QualityState(State):
    last_file: str = ""
    last_size: int = 0

    def handle_file(self, file=None):
        self.last_file = getattr(file, "filename", "")
        self.last_size = getattr(file, "size", 0)

app = App(title="Quality Console")

@app.page("/")
def quality():
    return data_quality_dashboard(
        score=97.5,
        metrics={"Last file size": f"{int(QualityState.last_size):,} bytes"},
        datasets=[
            {"Dataset": "orders", "Owner": "finance", "Status": "Healthy"},
        ],
        issues=[],
        upload=DataUpload(
            accept=".csv,.json,.parquet",
            on_upload=QualityState.handle_file,
        ),
    )

docs.title: ML engineers: compose custom evaluation widgets
docs.text:
Evaluation slots accept either structured dictionaries or your own PyDataUI components. This is useful when a metric needs a custom chart or annotation.

from pydataui.components.data_science import (
    ConfusionMatrix,
    FeatureImportance,
    PlotlyChart,
)
from pydataui.templates import model_registry

return model_registry(
    model={
        "name": "churn_classifier",
        "version": "v12",
        "stage": "production",
        "metrics": {"AUC": 0.985, "F1": 0.942},
    },
    confusion_matrix=ConfusionMatrix(
        matrix=[[100, 10], [5, 85]],
        labels=["Retained", "Churned"],
    ),
    feature_importance=FeatureImportance(
        features={"tenure": 0.45, "support_calls": 0.35},
        title="Drivers of churn",
    ),
    models=[
        {"Model": "churn_classifier", "Version": "v12", "Stage": "production"},
    ],
)

docs.title: Production Deployment
docs.text: Multi-Worker & Persistent Storage: PyDataUI v0.2.1 includes a zero-infrastructure SQLite WAL storage engine (pydataui.storage). For multi-worker deployments (--workers 4+) or container volume mounts, configure PYDATAUI_STORAGE=sqlite:///var/data/pydataui_storage.db or let PyDataUI auto-configure .pydataui_storage.db. Read the production readiness guide for architecture details.

docs.title: Production Deployment Guide
docs.text: PyDataUI is designed from the ground up for high-throughput production workloads. Built on the pyrustapi engine (Rust/Tokio/Hyper), it does not require external Python application servers like Uvicorn or Gunicorn.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
1. One-Click Docker Build via CLI
  2. Production Dockerfile
  3. Docker Compose Deployment
  4. Kubernetes Manifests
  5. Systemd Service (Linux Server)
  6. Nginx Reverse Proxy Configuration
  7. Environment Variables Reference
  8. Production Security Checklist

docs.title: 1. One-Click Docker Build via CLI
docs.text:
PyDataUI includes an automated build command that creates a production-ready container directory:

pydataui build app.py --output dist

This packages: - dist/app.py - dist/static/ (bundled HTMX & CSS assets) - dist/Dockerfile - dist/docker-compose.yml - dist/requirements.txt

Build and run: 

cd dist
docker compose up --build -d

docs.title: 2. Production Dockerfile
docs.text:
If creating your own Dockerfile:

FROM python:3.11-slim

# Install system dependencies
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    curl \
    build-essential \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

WORKDIR /app

# Install Python requirements
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Copy application files
COPY . .

# Set production environment variables
ENV PYDATAUI_HOST=0.0.0.0
ENV PYDATAUI_PORT=8000
ENV PYDATAUI_DEBUG=false
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

EXPOSE 8000

# Run with pyrustapi multi-worker engine
CMD ["pydataui", "run", "app.py", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000", "--workers", "1"]

docs.title: 3. Docker Compose Deployment
docs.text:
version: '3.8'

services:
  pydataui:
    build: .
    restart: always
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    environment:
      - PYDATAUI_HOST=0.0.0.0
      - PYDATAUI_PORT=8000
      - PYDATAUI_SESSION_SECRET=${PYDATAUI_SESSION_SECRET:-a-very-long-production-secret-token-min-32-chars}
      - PYDATAUI_SESSION_MAX_AGE=86400
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:8000/_pdu/health"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: '2.0'
          memory: 2048M

docs.title: 4. Kubernetes Manifests
docs.text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: pydataui-app
  labels:
    app: pydataui
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: pydataui
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: pydataui
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: your-registry.com/data/pydataui-app:v0.2.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
        env:
        - name: PYDATAUI_HOST
          value: "0.0.0.0"
        - name: PYDATAUI_PORT
          value: "8000"
        - name: PYDATAUI_SESSION_SECRET
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: pdu-secrets
              key: session-secret
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /_pdu/health
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /_pdu/health
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 2
          periodSeconds: 5
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "250m"
            memory: "256Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "1000m"
            memory: "1024Mi"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: pydataui-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8000
  selector:
    app: pydataui

docs.title: 5. Systemd Service (Linux Server)
docs.text:
Create /etc/systemd/system/pydataui.service:

[Unit]
Description=PyDataUI Production Service
After=network.target

[Service]
User=www-data
Group=www-data
WorkingDirectory=/var/www/my-pydataui-app
Environment="PATH=/var/www/my-pydataui-app/venv/bin"
Environment="PYDATAUI_HOST=127.0.0.1"
Environment="PYDATAUI_PORT=8000"
Environment="PYDATAUI_SESSION_SECRET=your-32-char-random-secret-key-here"
ExecStart=/var/www/my-pydataui-app/venv/bin/pydataui run app.py --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --workers 1
Restart=always
RestartSec=3

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Enable and start: 

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now pydataui

docs.title: 6. Nginx Reverse Proxy Configuration
docs.text:
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name analytics.company.internal;
    return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl http2;
    server_name analytics.company.internal;

    ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/analytics.company.internal/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/analytics.company.internal/privkey.pem;

    # Static assets cache
    location /_pdu/static/ {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        expires 7d;
        add_header Cache-Control "public, no-transform";
    }

    # Application & HTMX traffic
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

        # WebSocket / Long-lived requests
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
        proxy_read_timeout 300s;
    }
}

docs.title: 7. Environment Variables Reference
docs.text:
All PyDataUI settings can be configured via environment variables prefixed with PYDATAUI_:

Variable Default Description PYDATAUI_TITLE PyDataUI App Application browser title PYDATAUI_HOST 127.0.0.1 Network interface to bind to PYDATAUI_PORT 8000 Port number PYDATAUI_DEBUG false Enable verbose logging PYDATAUI_SESSION_SECRET Auto-generated Secret key for signing session cookies PYDATAUI_SESSION_MAX_AGE 86400 Session lifetime in seconds (24 hours) PYDATAUI_API_PREFIX /api Base path for auto-generated REST APIs PYDATAUI_THEME light Default theme: light or dark PYDATAUI_STORAGE Auto (memory or sqlite) Pluggable store (sqlite:///path/to/storage.db)

docs.title: 8. Production Security Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Secret Key: Set PYDATAUI_SESSION_SECRET to a high-entropy string (e.g. openssl rand -hex 32).
  • [ ] HTTPS: Terminate SSL/TLS at your load balancer or Nginx reverse proxy.
  • [ ] API Keys: Revoke test keys before promoting to production.
  • [ ] Multi-Worker Storage: Set PYDATAUI_STORAGE="sqlite:///path/to/storage.db" or let PyDataUI auto-configure .pydataui_storage.db when running multi-worker (--workers 4+).
  • [ ] CORS: Configure cors_origins in AppConfig to restrict cross-origin API calls.

docs.title: 📚 Documentation Developer Guide (Markdown, HTML & GitHub Pages)

docs.title: 🏗️ Architecture & Tooling
docs.text:
PyDataUI's documentation site is generated statically from Markdown and HTML source files using Material for MkDocs and deployed automatically via GitHub Pages.

+ HTML Snippets"] --> MkDocs["MkDocs Engine

Install the required packages in your Python virtual environment:

pip install mkdocs mkdocs-material pymdown-extensions

docs.title: 2. Start Live Development Server

Run mkdocs serve from the repository root:

mkdocs serve
  • Access the live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000/.
  • Any edits saved in docs/ or mkdocs.yml trigger instant hot-reload in your browser.

docs.title: 3. Verify Production Build
docs.text:
Ensure there are no broken links, unclosed tags, or missing navigation references:

mkdocs build --strict

docs.text:
Every time a commit is pushed to the main branch affecting documentation, the GitHub Actions workflow at .github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml triggers automatically:

  1. Trigger Condition:
  2. Push to branch main
  3. Modified paths: docs/**, mkdocs.yml, .github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml
  4. Or manual trigger via Actions ➡️ Deploy Documentation to GitHub Pages ➡️ Run workflow.

docs.title: HTML Reference for Developers
docs.text:
This guide covers the HTML contract behind PyDataUI: how Python components become markup, which semantic tags are available, how attributes are normalized, and where the security boundaries are. It is intended for application developers building custom layouts and for contributors extending the component system.

For the higher-level customization workflow, start with UI Customization & Tailwind. For design tokens and stylesheet internals, see the CSS Reference.

docs.title: 1. Rendering Model
docs.text:
PyDataUI does not use a client-side component runtime or a template language. Every component renders to an HTML string on the server.

Python component tree
        |
        v
Component.render(state_snapshot)
        |
        +--> _build_attrs()      ids, classes, styles, hx-* attributes
        +--> _render_children()  escaped text, child components, state values
        |
        v
HTML string
        |
        +--> full document shell (initial page load)
        +--> HTML fragment      (HTMX event response)

The main implementation points are:

File Responsibility pydataui/components/base.py Component, attribute rendering, escaping, child rendering, RawHtml pydataui/components/html.py Semantic HTML and SVG tag classes pydataui/compiler/templates.py Full document shell and application-level <head> pydataui/compiler/renderer.py Page and fragment rendering pydataui/utils.py escape_html, ID generation, value conversion

An HTMX event returns a fragment, not a complete page. The fragment is swapped into #pdu-root; therefore a component must render correctly both inside the initial document and on its own.

docs.title: 2. Document Shell
docs.text:
The application shell is generated by get_base_html() in pydataui/compiler/templates.py. Its relevant structure is:

<html class="dark"> <!-- only when App(theme="dark") -->
  <head>
    <script src="https://cdn.tailwindcss.com"></script>
    <script>tailwind.config = {...};</script>
    <style>
      :root { /* shadcn design tokens */ }
      /* custom_css */
    </style>
    <script src="/_pdu/static/htmx.min.js"></script>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="/_pdu/static/pydataui.css">
    <!-- App(stylesheets=[...]) -->
    <!-- App(head=...) -->
  </head>
  <body class="min-h-screen" hx-headers='{"X-CSRF-Token":"..."}'>
    <div id="pdu-root" class="min-h-screen">
      <!-- page content -->
    </div>
  </body>
</html>

Key contracts:

  • #pdu-root is the default HTMX target and the default hx-include source.
  • hx-headers on <body> carries the CSRF token for event requests.
  • App(stylesheets=[...]) loads after the framework stylesheet.
  • App(custom_css="...") is injected before HTMX and before pydataui.css.
  • App(head="...") is the last item in <head>.

docs.title: 3. Common Component Properties
docs.text:
Every Component accepts the following arguments:

Argument Output Notes id id="..." Generated as pdu-<8 hex chars> when omitted. Supply your own for anchors, labels, tests, or JavaScript hooks. class_name Appended to class="..." Framework classes come first, then your Tailwind or custom classes. style style="..." A string is emitted as-is. A dict is joined with ;. Numeric values receive a px suffix. Dict keys are literal CSS property names. hidden No output hidden=True removes the component and its subtree from the response; it does not render the HTML hidden attribute. **props HTML attributes snake_case becomes kebab-case; data_* becomes data-*. on_* HTMX attributes Event handlers are converted to hx-* attributes and are never emitted as inline JavaScript.

Examples:

from pydataui.html import Section, P

Section(
    P("Rendered with a custom class and inline width."),
    id="quality-panel",
    class_name="pdu-p-lg bg-slate-50",
    style={"max-width": "48rem", "margin-top": 16},
)

The numeric 16 becomes 16px.

docs.title: Attribute Normalization
docs.text:
Python input HTML output aria_label="Quality" aria-label="Quality" data_action="refresh" data-action="refresh" data_testid=True data-testid="" disabled=True disabled disabled=False Omitted required=True required class_name="mt-4" Appended to the generated class list

Boolean HTML attributes are emitted correctly instead of becoming disabled="False". Supported boolean attributes include disabled, required, readonly, checked, selected, autofocus, multiple, hidden, open, novalidate, defer, async, loop, autoplay, controls, and muted.

None and False prop values are omitted. Strings and other values are escaped before being written into attributes.

docs.title: 4. Semantic HTML Tags
docs.text:
Import tags from pydataui.html:

from pydataui.html import Section, Header, Nav, Main, Article, Aside, Footer
from pydataui.html import Div, Span, P, H1, H2, H3, H4, H5, H6
from pydataui.html import A, Ul, Ol, Li, Strong, Em, CodeTag, Pre, Hr, Br

docs.title: Structure and Text
docs.text: Class Element Purpose Div <div> Generic block container Span <span> Generic inline container Section <section> Thematic section Article <article> Self-contained content Header <header> Introductory content Footer <footer> Footer content Main <main> Primary page content Nav <nav> Navigation links Aside <aside> Complementary content P <p> Paragraph H1–H6 <h1>–<h6> Heading levels Strong <strong> Important text Em <em> Emphasized text CodeTag <code> Inline code Pre <pre> Preformatted block Hr <hr> Thematic break Br <br> Line break

docs.title: Links and Lists
docs.text:
Class Element Special arguments A <a> href (defaults to "#") Ul <ul> None Ol <ol> None Li <li> None 
A("View catalog", href="/catalog", target="_blank", rel="noopener")

docs.title: SVG
docs.text:
Class Element Special arguments Svg <svg> viewBox (default "0 0 24 24"), fill (default "none"), stroke (default "currentColor") Path <path> d Circle <circle> cx, cy, r Rect <rect> x, y, width, height Line <line> x1, y1, x2, y2 
from pydataui.html import Svg, Path

icon = Svg(
    Path(d="M13 10V3L4 14h7v7l9-11h-7z"),
    class_name="h-6 w-6 text-amber-500",
)

The optional Path, Circle, Rect, and Line coordinates are only added when truthy. Values such as viewBox are preserved with their HTML attribute casing.

docs.title: Forms
docs.text:
Class Element Special arguments FormTag <form> None; pass method, action, etc. as props ButtonTag <button> type (default "button") InputTag <input> type (default "text"); void element LabelTag <label> None TextareaTag <textarea> None SelectTag <select> None OptionTag <option> value

For for on a label, use a dict because for is a Python keyword:

LabelTag("Search", **{"for": "catalog-search"})
InputTag(id="catalog-search", type="search", name="q", placeholder="Search tables")

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
Class Element TableTag <table> TheadTag <thead> TbodyTag <tbody> TrTag <tr> ThTag <th> TdTag <td>

Use scope="col" or scope="row" on header cells for accessible tables.

docs.title: 5. Children, Values, and Escaping
docs.text:
Children can be components, strings, numbers, lists, tuples, None, StateVarRef values, or callables that accept the state snapshot.

from pydataui.html import Article, H2, P

Article(
    H2("Orders"),
    "Today's volume: ",
    1250,
    P("Compared with yesterday: ", order_delta),
)

Rendering rules:

  • None children are skipped.
  • Nested lists and tuples are flattened one level.
  • Component children render recursively.
  • User-provided text is escaped with html.escape(..., quote=True).
  • Attribute values are escaped before output.
  • Callable children are invoked with the state snapshot.
  • StateVarRef children resolve against the current state snapshot.

This means this input:

P("Use <table> & <script> safely")

produces escaped text content, not executable markup:

<p id="pdu-..." class="pdu">Use <table> & <script> safely</p>

docs.title: Raw HTML
docs.text:
RawHtml and its alias Html bypass escaping:

from pydataui import Html

Html('<div class="trusted-embed">...</div>')

Only use these for trusted templates, pre-sanitized content, or third-party embeds you control. Do not pass user input directly to RawHtml. Prefer normal components for user-derived values.

docs.title: 6. Complete Rendered Example
docs.text:
from pydataui.html import Section, H1, P, A, ButtonTag

Section(
    H1("Quality overview"),
    P("All checks passed.", class_name="text-muted-foreground"),
    A("Open catalog", href="/catalog", target="_blank", rel="noopener"),
    ButtonTag("Refresh", type="button", data_action="refresh", disabled=False),
    class_name="pdu-p-lg",
    style={"max-width": "48rem"},
)

Representative output (IDs vary per instance):

<section id="pdu-55a67749" class="pdu pdu-p-lg" style="max-width: 48rem">
  <h1 id="pdu-66d947a8" class="pdu">Quality overview</h1>
  <p id="pdu-ab69fb02" class="pdu text-muted-foreground">All checks passed.</p>
  <a id="pdu-f024984e" class="pdu" target="_blank" rel="noopener" href="/catalog">Open catalog</a>
  <button id="pdu-ed1fcf83" class="pdu" data-action="refresh" type="button">Refresh</button>
</section>

Every component receives the base pdu class. Framework components append their own classes, and class_name is appended last.

docs.title: 7. State and Event Attributes
docs.text:
State values can appear in text, props, and attributes:

from pydataui import State
from pydataui.html import P, ButtonTag

class CounterState(State):
    count: int = 0

    def increment(self):
        self.count += 1

P("Count: ", CounterState.count)
ButtonTag("Increment", on_click=CounterState.increment)

Event handlers render as HTMX attributes:

<button
  id="pdu-e918535d"
  class="pdu"
  hx-post="/_pdu/event/CounterState/increment"
  hx-target="#pdu-root"
  hx-swap="innerHTML"
  hx-trigger="click"
  hx-include="#pdu-root"
  type="button">Increment</button>

Do not hand-write these hx-* attributes for state methods. Use on_click=, on_change=, and the other supported event arguments so routing and CSRF behavior stay consistent.

docs.title: 8. Extending HTML Components
docs.text:
Subclass Component to add a semantic wrapper or a project-specific primitive:

from pydataui import Component

class StatusPill(Component):
    tag = "span"

    def __init__(self, label, tone="success", **kwargs):
        super().__init__(label, **kwargs)
        self.tone = tone

    def _get_classes(self):
        return super()._get_classes() + [
            "pdu-badge",
            f"pdu-badge-{self.tone}",
        ]

Usage:

StatusPill("Healthy")

Keep behavior server-side. If a component needs interactivity, express it through state methods and event handlers rather than injecting JavaScript. For a full CSS component checklist, see Extending the CSS Layer.

docs.title: 9. Accessibility Checklist
docs.text:
• Prefer semantic elements (button, nav, main, section, table) over generic div structures.
  • Always provide a type for ButtonTag; the default is "button", which avoids accidental form submission.
  • Associate labels and inputs with matching id/for values.
  • Use table headers with scope="col" or scope="row".
  • Give SVGs a title or aria-label when they convey meaning; mark decorative SVGs with aria-hidden="true".
  • Do not put click handlers on non-interactive elements. Use a button or link.
  • Test keyboard navigation and visible focus states after overriding framework colors.
  • Keep class_name changes from removing focus outlines unless you provide a replacement.

docs.title: 10. Testing HTML and Security
docs.text:
Unit-test rendered markup without starting a server:

from pydataui.html import P, Section

def test_quality_section_escapes_user_text():
    html = Section(P("<script>alert(1)</script>")).render({})
    assert "<script>" not in html
    assert "<script>" in html

Useful test patterns:

  • Call .render({}) and assert on stable IDs, classes, and escaped content.
  • Pass an explicit id when asserting on a specific element.
  • Test hidden=True, boolean attributes, and data_* conversion.
  • Add browser coverage for layout, HTMX swaps, and responsive behavior.
  • Never use RawHtml with untrusted test fixtures unless the test is specifically verifying sanitization.
