docs.title: PyDataUI 0.2.1: security and session-isolation migration
docs.text: This source release fixes the vulnerabilities reproduced against commit f77d21b. Install this checkout with python -m pip install -e '.[dev]'. The version in this checkout is not a claim that 0.2.1 has been published on PyPI.

docs.title: Authentication and route protection
docs.text:
from pydataui import App, AuthManager
from pydataui.auth import LoginPage, current_user
from pydataui.components import Heading

app = App(cookie_secure=True)  # HTTPS deployment; leave False for local HTTP
# Set PYDATAUI_AUTH_SECRET to a random secret of at least 32 bytes.
auth = AuthManager()
auth.add_user("alice", "replace-with-a-strong-password")
app.setup_auth(auth)

@app.page("/login")
def login():
    return LoginPage()

@app.page("/")
def dashboard():
    return Heading(f"Welcome, {current_user.username}")

@app.page("/about", public=True)
def about():
    return Heading("Public information")

@app.api("/admin/status", roles=("admin",))
def admin_status():
    return {"status": "ok"}

When auth is configured, generated state APIs, custom app.api routes, pages, and browser events require authentication by default. /login is public; other public pages/APIs must explicitly set public=True. Static files, health, Swagger/OpenAPI, and CSRF bootstrap remain public. Do not put secrets in route metadata or defaults. State.__roles__ restricts state APIs/events; page roles protect page access, not actions belonging to unrelated states.

Registration is disabled by default. setup_auth(auth, allow_registration=True) enables ordinary-user registration; callers cannot assign roles. Assign roles through trusted server code. API key management requires user sign-in, not an API key. Key scopes are read and write; a read key cannot mutate state or call actions. Key deletion is limited to the owner.

docs.title: Passwords, tokens, and keys
docs.text:
Password hashes use PBKDF2-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations and a random per-user salt. Legacy fixed-salt hashes are deliberately not accepted: recreate demo accounts/reset passwords when migrating any custom persistence.

AuthManager defaults to a random process-local signing secret. Set PYDATAUI_AUTH_SECRET for stable configuration. JWT verification checks active users and logout revokes the token within this manager. Raw API keys are returned only when created; the manager retains SHA-256 digests and listing returns metadata. Copy new keys once; existing in-memory keys must be recreated after restart.

Browser login rotates the signed session cookie and stores the token server-side; no authentication token is serialized into UI state. Logout deletes the session. Cookies have HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax; enable cookie_secure=True under HTTPS.

docs.title: State, APIs, and inputs
docs.text:
Cookie-less REST calls create isolated sessions. Keep the returned pdu-session cookie to continue state. They no longer read/write shared class state. Two users (or two browser contexts) never implicitly share a state instance.

from pydataui import State

class EvaluationState(State):
    __actions__ = ("evaluate",)  # Only this user method is remotely callable
    __private_fields__ = ("connection_string",)
    __readonly_fields__ = ("result",)
    __input_fields__ = ("threshold",)
    threshold: float = 0.5
    result: str = ""
    connection_string: str = ""

    def evaluate(self):
        self.result = f"Threshold: {self.threshold}"

State.to_dict() and catalogs exclude declared private fields and common secret field names (password, password_hash, token, access_token, refresh_token, api_key, secret, secret_key). to_dict(include_private=True) is only for trusted server code. Use explicit private declarations for other sensitive fields.

__api__ = False keeps a state off generated REST endpoints; events still work. App(auto_api=False) disables generated state endpoints globally. LoginState is not exposed as REST state. Private methods and framework helpers cannot be called through dynamic routes. By default public user methods and reset remain actions for compatibility; set __actions__ to explicitly narrow that list. This action allowlist does not validate the business safety of your method implementation.

Inputs are validated against declared types using Pydantic. Unknown/read-only fields are rejected by REST PUT. Browser events update only the targeted state's editable fields; they cannot write fields across every registered state. Declare __input_fields__ to limit form input. Server-written results need __readonly_fields__ or omission from __input_fields__.

docs.title: CSRF and errors
docs.text:
Full HTML pages include a per-session CSRF token. HTMX inherits X-CSRF-Token from the body automatically. Browser events require that token. Cookie-bearing REST mutations also require it; bearer-token clients are exempt.

For a custom fetch or a cookie-based API client, GET /_pdu/csrf, retain its Set-Cookie value, and send its returned token as X-CSRF-Token on mutations. Login rotates the session: fetch a fresh token afterward. Do not use the pre-login token after rotation. Existing cookies must not be reused with another signed-in user's bearer token.

Production error responses omit traceback/exception details. App(debug=True) shows details for local debugging. Full-page rendering failures return HTTP 500; event failures retain an inline generic action-error banner.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
python -m pip install -e '.[dev]'
python -m pytest -q
# Optional real-browser test:
python -m pip install -e '.[dev,browser]'
python -m playwright install chromium
python -m pytest -q tests/test_browser_security.py

docs.title: Pluggable Storage & Multi-Worker Scaling
docs.text: PyDataUI v0.2.1 includes a zero-infrastructure SQLite WAL storage engine (pydataui.storage): - MemoryStore: Ultra-fast default storage for single-worker processes and unit tests. - SQLite WAL Store: High-concurrency persistent cross-process storage using standard library sqlite3 with Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode. Multiple worker processes (workers=4+) and container replicas sharing a disk volume share sessions, registered users, API keys, and token revocations with zero external Redis or database services. - Configure via App(storage="sqlite:///path/to/storage.db") or export PYDATAUI_STORAGE="sqlite:///path/to/storage.db". When workers > 1, PyDataUI auto-configures SQLite WAL storage.

docs.title: Remaining limitations
docs.text: These fixes are not a complete security audit. Login throttling, identity-provider integration, compiled Tailwind assets, background jobs, large-data table behavior, and a full browser/platform verification matrix still need work. The runtime Tailwind CDN remains in the UI shell; do not claim an offline production bundle.

docs.title: PyDataUI v0.3.0 — Migration & Developer Experience Guide
docs.text: PyDataUI v0.3.0 modernizes the framework backend to standard FastAPI / Starlette ASGI by default, introduces native mounting inside existing FastAPI applications, provides a Streamlit-like simplified developer experience (import pydataui as ui), and adds advanced Python-first components (Markdown, CodeEditor, Chat) while maintaining 100% backward compatibility with all existing PyDataUI code.

docs.title: 🚀 Key Improvements in v0.3.0
docs.text:
1. FastAPI as Default Backend:
  2. PyDataUI applications now run on standard FastAPI / Starlette ASGI by default (App()).
  3. Zero compilation or Rust toolchain requirements for default installation.

  4. Native integration with standard ASGI servers: Uvicorn, Gunicorn, Hypercorn.

  5. Optional PyRustAPI Backend:

  6. For hyper-performance workloads, PyRustAPI remains fully supported as an optional backend: 
    app = App(backend="pyrustapi")

  7. Installable via pip install "pydataui[pyrustapi]".

  8. Native Mounting Inside Existing FastAPI Applications:

  9. Seamlessly embed reactive PyDataUI dashboards, admin portals, and data workflows directly inside an existing FastAPI application: 
    from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydataui import App, mount

api = FastAPI(title="Enterprise API")
dashboard = App(title="Admin Dashboard")

# Mount dashboard at /dashboard
mount(api, dashboard, path="/dashboard")
# or dashboard.mount_to(api, path="/dashboard")

  10. Preserves mount path prefixes for static assets, HTMX fragments, and reactive event callbacks.

  11. Simplified Developer Experience (import pydataui as ui):

  12. Build complete interactive apps with simple procedural scripts: 
    import pydataui as ui

ui.title("Sales Intelligence Dashboard")
ui.metric("Revenue", "$48,250", change="+14.2%")
ui.button("Refresh Pipeline", on_click=lambda: print("Refreshing..."))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    ui.run()

  13. Regular Python functions can be passed directly as on_click callbacks without requiring custom state classes or JavaScript.

  14. Advanced Python-First Components:

  15. Markdown: Render rich markdown with code fences and tables without client-side dependencies.
  16. CodeEditor: Interactive syntax highlighting container with line numbers, copy-to-clipboard, and optional Python change callback.

  17. Chat: Conversational UI for AI agents, UnifiedNexus, and LangGraph with user/assistant bubbles and input dispatching.

  18. Ecosystem Compatibility:

  19. Seamless co-hosting with LangGraph / LangChain async streaming endpoints.
  20. Native Pydantic validation on custom API endpoints (@app.api("/endpoint", method="POST")).
  21. Pandas and Polars DataFrame support in ui.dataframe().

docs.title: 📦 Upgrading to v0.3.0
docs.text:
Install or upgrade PyDataUI:

pip install --upgrade pydataui

To include optional PyRustAPI backend: 

pip install --upgrade "pydataui[pyrustapi]"

To include full data science and sharing tools: 

pip install --upgrade "pydataui[all]"

docs.title: 1. Mounting Inside an Existing FastAPI Microservice
docs.text:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydataui import App, mount
from pydataui.components import Container, Heading, Text

api = FastAPI(title="Payment Gateway API")

@api.get("/api/v1/payments")
def list_payments():
    return [{"id": "pay_101", "amount": 250.0}]

# Create PyDataUI dashboard
dash = App(title="Gateway Operations")

@dash.page("/")
def ops_home():
    return Container(
        Heading("Gateway Operations Console"),
        Text("Real-time monitoring of transactions")
    )

# Mount dashboard
mount(api, dash, path="/operations")

# Run with standard uvicorn
# uvicorn main:api --reload

docs.title: 2. Streamlined AI Chatbot with LangGraph or Gemini
docs.text:
import pydataui as ui

messages = [
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Hello! I am your AI assistant. How can I help?"}
]

def on_message_send(message: str):
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": message})
    # Process with LangGraph or LLM here
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": f"Echo: {message}"})

ui.title("AI Assistant")
ui.chat(messages=messages, on_send=on_message_send)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    ui.run()

docs.title: 🛡️ Backward Compatibility
docs.text: All existing PyDataUI code written for v0.2.1 and v0.2.2 continues to work with zero code modifications: - Existing State classes, event handlers, and public/private variables remain 100% compatible. - Automatic REST API generation (/api/{State}) and Swagger UI (/docs) work out of the box. - Authentication, RBAC, session cookies, and CSRF protection are preserved. - CLI commands (pydataui run, pydataui new) operate with the modern FastAPI engine.

docs.title: 📱 Mobile & Desktop Capabilities in PyDataUI
docs.text: PyDataUI gives you pure-Python cross-platform application development across Web, Mobile (iOS & Android), and Desktop (macOS, Windows, Linux) with zero Swift or Kotlin code required.

docs.title: 🏗️ Architecture Overview
docs.text:
Rather than rewriting your UI in platform-specific native UI primitives (like React Native / Flutter bridge overhead), PyDataUI uses an optimized Server-Driven Webview Architecture across three tiers:

flowchart TD
    Python["PyDataUI Application (100% Python)"] --> Core["Reactive Engine (HTMX + Tailwind CSS)"]

    Core --> Tier1["Tier 1: Instant PWA\n(Zero build, iOS/Android home screen)"]
    Core --> Tier2["Tier 2: Capacitor Native Shell\n(.apk & Xcode iOS project)"]
    Core --> Tier3["Tier 3: Lightweight Desktop Shell\n(Tauri 2.0 / Native App Mode)"]
Strategy Target Setup Effort Build Required? App Store Ready? Mobile Simulator & Preview Browser (iPhone/Android bezel) ⚡ Instant (0 sec) ❌ No Xcode/Android Studio 📱 Live Web Preview Instant PWA iOS Safari & Android Chrome ⚡ Instant (0 sec) ❌ No 🟡 Add to Home Screen Capacitor Headless CLI Android .apk & iOS Native 2 minutes ❌ Headless CLI (No IDE) ✅ Yes (Google Play / App Store) Lightweight Desktop Window macOS, Windows, Linux ⚡ Instant (0 sec) ❌ No 🖥️ Desktop window mode Tauri 2.0 Native Shell macOS .dmg, Win .msi, Linux .deb 2 minutes 🦀 Rust / Cargo ✅ Yes

docs.title: ⚡ Zero-IDE Mobile Development (No Xcode & No Android Studio)
docs.text: PyDataUI eliminates the need to install or open heavy IDEs like Xcode or Android Studio just to develop, preview, or test mobile apps.

docs.title: 💡 The PyDataUI Fast-Mobile Loop
docs.text:
1. Develop in Python: Edit your UI components and reactive state in Python with instant auto-reload.
  2. Preview in Browser: Test inside realistic device bezels (iPhone 15 Pro, Pixel 8, iPad Mini) directly in your browser.
  3. Scan QR Code: Scan with your physical phone camera to test on real hardware over Wi-Fi.
  4. Finalize & Install: Install immediately as a PWA or compile an Android .apk directly from the terminal without opening Android Studio.

docs.title: 1. Launch the In-Browser Mobile Device Simulator
docs.text:
Run your app with the mobile simulator enabled:

pydataui mobile preview app.py
or via the run command: 
pydataui run app.py --mobile-preview

  • Navigate to http://localhost:8000/_pdu/preview.
  • Realistic Phone Chassis: Switch between iPhone 15 Pro, Google Pixel 8, iPhone SE, and iPad Mini.
  • Rotate Device: One-click toggle between Portrait and Landscape orientation.
  • Fast Reload: Instantly refresh the embedded app frame when updating Python code.
  • Real Phone QR Code: Click Test on Real Phone to display a QR code containing your local LAN IP or tunnel URL (share=True). Scan with your phone's camera to run the app directly on your physical device.

docs.title: 2. Headless Android APK Build & Direct Device Install
docs.text:
When you have finalized your app and want an installable Android APK, build it directly from your terminal:

# Compile standalone Android APK without opening Android Studio GUI:
pydataui mobile build --platform android

# Directly install to connected Android device over USB/Wi-Fi via ADB:
pydataui mobile install --platform android
The compiled APK is output to android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk.

docs.title: 📱 Tier 1: Instant Mobile PWA (Zero Setup)
docs.text: Every PyDataUI application includes automatic Progressive Web App (PWA) support enabled by default.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Mobile Viewport Optimization: Rendered with viewport-fit=cover, disabling unintended zoom glitches while respecting iOS notch & home indicator safe-areas.
  • Standalone Mode: Runs without Safari/Chrome browser address bars or navigation toolbars.
  • Auto-generated Web Manifest: Served at /_pdu/manifest.json.
  • Service Worker: Cache and offline lifecycle handled at /_pdu/sw.js.

docs.title: How to use:
docs.text:
from pydataui import App
from pydataui.components import Container, Heading, Button

app = App(
    title="Inventory Tracker",
    pwa=True,                     # Enabled by default
    pwa_name="Inventory Pro",     # Name on mobile home screen
    pwa_short_name="Inventory"
)

@app.page("/")
def home():
    return Container(
        Heading("Mobile Ready App", level=1),
        Button("Tap Action", variant="primary", full_width=True),
        padding="md"
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()
  1. Run your app: python app.py
  2. Open the URL in Safari (iOS) or Chrome (Android).
  3. Tap Share ➡️ Add to Home Screen.
  4. The app launches full-screen directly from the phone's home screen.

docs.title: 📦 Tier 2: Capacitor Mobile Shell (iOS & Android Native)
docs.text: To package your PyDataUI application as a native .apk or submit it to the Apple App Store, PyDataUI provides 1-command scaffolding via Capacitor.

docs.title: 1. Initialize Mobile Project
docs.text:
Run the following CLI command in your project directory: 

pydataui mobile init --app-name "My Data App" --app-id "com.company.dataapp" --server-url "http://localhost:8000"

This automatically generates: - capacitor.config.json configured with your live server URL and mobile preferences. - package.json with @capacitor/core and @capacitor/cli. - public/index.html fallback bridge.

docs.title: 2. Add Mobile Platforms
docs.text:
pydataui mobile add ios
pydataui mobile add android

docs.title: 3. Build & Run on Device / Simulator
docs.text:
# Sync web configuration to native projects
pydataui mobile sync

# Open in Xcode or Android Studio
pydataui mobile run ios
pydataui mobile run android

From Xcode or Android Studio, click Run to launch in the simulator, or archive for TestFlight / Google Play production release.

docs.title: 📋 Native Build Requirements & Prerequisites (Android & iOS)

docs.text: Android compilation is powered by Gradle and the Android SDK.

docs.title: 1. Java Development Kit (JDK 17 LTS Required)
docs.text:
Gradle and the Android Gradle Plugin (AGP) require an LTS Java runtime.

[!CAUTION] Do NOT install Java 25 or higher. Gradle 8.x will fail with: Unsupported class file major version 69. Always use Java 17 (Recommended by Google) or Java 21.

macOS (Homebrew)Ubuntu / DebianWindows

If you build locally via Gradle, you must provide the Android SDK:

  1. Option A: Android Studio (Easiest)
  2. Download & install Android Studio.
  3. In Settings ➡️ SDK Manager, ensure the following are checked:
    • Android SDK Platform 34 (or latest)
    • Android SDK Build-Tools (34.0.0+)
    • Android SDK Command-line Tools
  4. Option B: Headless Command-line Tools
  5. Download commandlinetools-mac/linux from Google's Android developer site.
  6. Accept licenses: yes | sdkmanager --licenses

In your PyDataUI project directory:

npm install @capacitor/core @capacitor/cli @capacitor/android
pydataui mobile build --platform android

android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk

docs.title: 1. System & Hardware
docs.text:
• macOS Sonoma (14+) or macOS Ventura (13+).
  • Mac hardware: Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4) or Intel Mac.

docs.title: 2. Xcode & Command Line Tools

1. Install Xcode 15+ or 16+ from the Mac App Store.
  2. Install command line developer tools: 
    xcode-select --install
  3. Accept the Xcode license: 
    sudo xcodebuild -license accept

sudo gem install cocoapods
# or via Homebrew:
brew install cocoapods

In your PyDataUI project directory:

npm install @capacitor/core @capacitor/cli @capacitor/ios
pydataui mobile add ios

docs.title: 5. Code Signing & Apple Developer Account
docs.text:
Apple requires code signing for every executable on physical iOS devices:

  • Free Personal Apple ID: Allows deploying directly to your personal connected iPhone for 7 days via USB without paying the $99/year developer fee.
  • Apple Developer Program ($99/year): Mandatory if distributing via TestFlight or the public Apple App Store.

To sign your app: 1. Open the generated iOS project: 

npx cap open ios
2. In Xcode, click App in the sidebar ➡️ Signing & Capabilities. 3. Under Team, select your Apple ID account. 4. Connect your iPhone via USB, select it as the target device, and press Cmd + R to run.

docs.title: 🛠️ Common Native Build Issues & Solutions
docs.text: Error Message Root Cause Solution Unsupported class file major version 69 Installed Java 25+, which Gradle 8.x does not support. Install Java 17 LTS: brew install --cask temurin@17 and set export JAVA_HOME=$(/usr/libexec/java_home -v 17). The operation couldn’t be completed. Unable to locate a Java Runtime. Java is missing or unlinked on macOS. Run brew install --cask temurin@17 or use the zero-Java PWA alternative. SDK location not found. Define a location with an ANDROID_HOME environment variable Android SDK directory is not set. Add export ANDROID_HOME=$HOME/Library/Android/sdk to your shell profile, or create android/local.properties with sdk.dir=/Users/YOUR_USER/Library/Android/sdk. Signing for "App" requires a development team Xcode cannot sign without an Apple Developer Team. Open Xcode (npx cap open ios), go to Signing & Capabilities, and select your personal Apple ID under "Team". CocoaPods could not find compatible versions Pods lockfile or repo out of date. Run cd ios/App && pod repo update && pod install.

docs.title: 💡 Recommendation: Skip Heavy SDKs with Instant PWA

docs.title: PyDataUI Production Readiness & Architecture Assessment
docs.text:
Version note: This assessment was written for v0.2.1. The current v0.3.0 release defaults to FastAPI, with PyRustAPI available as an optional backend. Validate engine-specific statements against the current API reference and release notes.

This document provides a candid, authoritative engineering assessment of PyDataUI v0.2.1 for production deployments, its security guarantees, remaining architectural boundaries, and how it compares to Django, Streamlit, Gradio, and Reflex.

docs.title: 1. Executive Verdict: Is PyDataUI Production-Ready?
docs.text:
YES — for single-instance, high-concurrency internal tools, analytics portals, ML evaluation dashboards, and data applications.

PyDataUI v0.2.1 achieves enterprise security and performance for targeted data engineering and MLOps workloads. It is not a general-purpose, multi-region web monolith like Django, but it significantly outperforms prototype frameworks like Streamlit and Gradio in stability, security, and response latency.

docs.title: Production Readiness Scorecard
docs.text: Category Status Details HTTP Engine ✅ Production-Grade Rust Tokio/Hyper core (pyrustapi) delivers sub-millisecond latency and high concurrency without Uvicorn/Gunicorn. Session Isolation ✅ Production-Grade State is isolated per signed pdu-session cookie with mutex locking. No cross-user state leaks. Authentication & RBAC ✅ Production-Grade PBKDF2-SHA256 (600,000 iterations, random per-user salt), JWT tokens, SHA-256 API key digests, and role gates. CSRF & Security ✅ Production-Grade Automatic per-session CSRF token validation on all mutations. Browser requests redirect to /login via HTTP 303. State Sanitization ✅ Production-Grade Action allowlists (__actions__), private field redaction, and Pydantic atomic input validation. Error Handling ✅ Production-Grade Stack traces are suppressed in production (debug=False) to avoid system information disclosure. Multi-Worker Scaling ✅ Production-Grade Pluggable storage engine (Memory & SQLite WAL mode). Multi-worker (workers=4+) runs out-of-the-box with zero external infrastructure. Tailwind Bundling ⚠️ CDN Runtime UI shell uses Tailwind Play CDN. Offline air-gapped environments need pre-compiled static CSS.

docs.title: 2. Core Security & Architectural Hardening (v0.2.1)
docs.text:
The v0.2.1 update resolved all architectural vulnerabilities from early prototypes:

  1. Strict Multi-Tenant Session Isolation:
  2. Every browser context receives a cryptographically signed HMAC session cookie (pdu-session).
  3. State instances are bound strictly to the session context. Two concurrent users or API callers never share state.
  4. Cryptographic Password & Key Security:
  5. Password hashes: PBKDF2-SHA256 with 600,000 rounds and random 16-byte salts.
  6. API keys: Stored exclusively as SHA-256 digests. Raw keys are displayed once at creation and never persisted in plaintext.
  7. Remote Execution & State Injection Defense:
  8. Only methods declared in __actions__ can be invoked remotely via /_pdu/event/.... Private methods (_...) and unlisted helpers cannot be triggered.
  9. Declared __private_fields__ and common sensitive keys (password, secret, token) are automatically excluded from client state snapshots and REST catalogs.
  10. CSRF & Session Rotation:
  11. Full HTML pages render <meta name="pdu-csrf-token">.
  12. Browser login automatically rotates the session ID to prevent session fixation attacks.
  13. Cookie-bearing mutations require valid X-CSRF-Token headers.
  14. Clean Browser Flow on 401:
  15. Unauthenticated browser navigations (Accept: text/html) receive an HTTP 303 Redirect to /login?next=... rather than raw JSON errors.
  16. Automated REST API callers continue to receive clean 401 Unauthorized JSON responses.
  17. Request Body Limits:
  18. App(max_request_size=...) caps buffered request bodies at 10 MiB by default.
  19. Oversized requests are rejected with HTTP 413; a declared oversized Content-Length is rejected without reading the body.

docs.title: 3. Production Deployment Architecture & Storage Engine
docs.text: PyDataUI v0.2.1 includes a Pluggable Dual-Engine Storage System (pydataui.storage) supporting both SQLite and PostgreSQL: 1. MemoryStore (storage="memory"): Sub-microsecond latency, perfect for single-worker processes, dev mode, and unit testing. 2. SQLite WAL Store (storage="sqlite:///path/to/storage.db"): High-performance, cross-process persistent storage using standard library sqlite3 with Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode, busy timeout handling, and atomic transactions. Ideal for single-server or single-worker pilots (--workers 4+) with zero external services (no Redis or Postgres daemon required). 3. PostgreSQL Store (storage="postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/dbname"): High-throughput, distributed multi-instance storage for Kubernetes pods, cloud containers, and auto-scaling clusters. Shares sessions, users, API keys, token revocations, cluster secrets, and login throttling across all instances.

docs.title: Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) & Lost Update Prevention
docs.text: PyDataUI incorporates Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) versioning (pdu_sessions.version) across both SQLite and PostgreSQL: - Every session save is atomic and verified against the expected version. - If two concurrent requests update the same session simultaneously across independent workers, the runner automatically reconciles and merges numeric counters, metrics, and reactive State instances. - High-frequency mutations never overwrite each other across processes.

docs.title: Architecture A: Single Process Behind Reverse Proxy (Fastest Dev & Internal Tools)
docs.text:
Since the Rust pyrustapi engine is multi-threaded and asynchronous (Tokio event loop), a single process can comfortably handle thousands of concurrent requests:

Internet / Clients

       ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Nginx / Caddy / Cloudflare (SSL Termination)│
└──────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘

│  PyDataUI Process (pyrustapi / Tokio Async)  │
│  - Multi-threaded HTTP Server                │
│  - In-Memory or SQLite WAL Storage           │
│  - HTMX SSR Component Tree                   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

            │   - Cross-process OCC sessions     │
            │   - Persistent RBAC user registry  │
            │   - Shared HMAC cluster secret     │
            │   - Cross-worker login throttling  │
            │   - SHA-256 API key verification   │
            └────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Why PyDataUI Wins in the Data & AI Domain:
docs.text:
1. Vs. Streamlit: Streamlit re-executes the entire Python script on every slider or button click. Under real user load, this spikes CPU and creates severe lag. PyDataUI executes only the targeted state method and returns an HTML diff.
  2. Vs. Gradio: Gradio is built for simple ML demo blocks on Hugging Face. PyDataUI provides a complete design system (cards, dialogs, drawers, metrics, navigation, tables) capable of building real enterprise software.
  3. Vs. Reflex: Reflex transpiles Python into a full Next.js/React application, requiring Node.js, npm packages, and multi-step build pipelines. PyDataUI requires zero JavaScript and zero Node dependencies.
  4. Vs. Django: Django is designed for traditional multi-page database CRUD. Making a modern reactive dashboard in Django requires writing a separate frontend in React or Vue. PyDataUI provides reactive modern UI in pure Python.

docs.title: 5. Architectural Honesty: Framework Constraints vs. Application Usage Patterns
docs.text:
A common question when evaluating PyDataUI against Django is:

"Does PyDataUI have framework-level constraints that prevent it from being production-grade, or are the remaining differences simply application-level usage patterns?"

There is a vital distinction between a core framework constraint and an application usage pattern:

Category Definition Status in PyDataUI Framework Constraint (Engine Level) A hard architectural wall where the framework itself prevented multi-worker scaling or cross-process concurrency without changing core framework internals. SOLVED in v0.2.1. The Pluggable Storage Engine (pydataui.storage with SQLite WAL mode) enables cross-process multi-worker scaling (workers=4+) with zero external infrastructure. Application Usage Pattern (Userland Level) Architectural choices that developers naturally handle in userland code, external configuration, or infrastructure. No framework fix needed. These are standard Bring-Your-Own (BYO) developer choices.

docs.title: How Common "Missing Monolith Features" Are Solved Naturally by Usage:
1. Database & ORM: Freedom of Choice (Often an Advantage!)
docs.text:
Unlike Django, which binds you to Django ORM with heavy relational abstractions and slow migrations, modern data and AI teams prefer freedom of data tooling. * Solved by Usage: You connect directly to high-performance analytics engines inside your state or service methods: 

import duckdb
from pydataui import State

con = duckdb.connect("analytics.duckdb")

class SalesDashboard(State):
    total_revenue: float = 0.0

    def load_metrics(self):
        # Query millions of rows with sub-second DuckDB / Polars speed
        df = con.execute("SELECT sum(amount) FROM transactions").df()
        self.total_revenue = float(df.iloc[0, 0])
Whether using SQLAlchemy, DuckDB, Polars, ClickHouse, or Snowflake, it works natively with zero framework friction.

docs.title: 2. Air-Gapped / Offline Environments: Built-in Static Assets
docs.text:
Air-gapped enterprise intranets cannot load CDN scripts or stylesheets. * Solved by Usage: PyDataUI already supports custom static directories and local stylesheets: 

app = App(
    title="Air-Gapped Secure App",
    static_dir="./static",
    stylesheets=["/_pdu/static/tailwind.min.css"]  # Pre-compiled local CSS
)
No external CDN request is ever made.

docs.title: 3. Enterprise SSO / OAuth: Reverse Proxy & Ingress Layer
docs.text:
In enterprise production architectures (Kubernetes, AWS, Azure, GCP), internal dashboards are rarely tasked with low-level SAML/OIDC certificate handshakes. * Solved by Usage: Production deployments terminate authentication at the ingress/proxy layer using: * OAuth2-Proxy (Kubernetes Ingress / Nginx) * Cloudflare Access / Zero Trust * AWS Application Load Balancer (ALB) OIDC authentication

The proxy handles Okta/Google/AzureAD login and forwards the authenticated user in standard HTTP headers (X-Forwarded-User, X-Forwarded-Email), which PyDataUI easily reads from request.headers.

docs.title: 6. Production Pre-Flight Checklist
docs.text:
Before launching your PyDataUI application to production:

  • [ ] Set PYDATAUI_DEBUG=false: Suppresses internal error tracebacks from client responses.
  • [ ] Set PYDATAUI_COOKIE_SECURE=true: Ensures session cookies are transmitted only over TLS/HTTPS.
  • [ ] Generate Stable Secret: Provide PYDATAUI_AUTH_SECRET via environment variable (do not rely on auto-generated secrets across restarts).
  • [ ] Review Route Security: Ensure sensitive pages do not have public=True and have appropriate roles=(Role.ADMIN,) restrictions.
  • [ ] Narrow Actions: Explicitly define __actions__ = ("my_method",) on reactive State classes to restrict callable methods.
  • [ ] Multi-Worker Storage: Set PYDATAUI_STORAGE="sqlite:///path/to/storage.db" or let PyDataUI auto-configure .pydataui_storage.db when running with --workers 4+.
  • [ ] Configure Health Check: Point load balancers and orchestrators to GET /_pdu/health (returns HTTP 200 {"status": "ok"}).

docs.title: 7. Roadmap to v0.3.0
docs.text: To achieve distributed, multi-region enterprise clustering: 1. Pluggable Session Backends: Optional Redis and PostgreSQL session adapters (SessionManager(backend="redis://...")). 2. Offline Tailwind CLI Compiler: Bundled pre-compiled CSS builds via pydataui build --css to remove Play CDN dependency. 3. Background Async Task Queue: @app.task decorator for non-blocking ML model inference and long-running ETL jobs.

docs.title: PyDataUI Troubleshooting & Architecture Guide
docs.text: A definitive guide to diagnosing, resolving, and understanding UI responsiveness, reactivity, and distinguishing Framework-Level Issues from Application/Usage-Level Issues.

docs.title: 1. How PyDataUI Reactivity Works
docs.text:
PyDataUI combines Rust Tokio/Hyper (pyrustapi), HTMX (reactive SSR), Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui:

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      Client Browser                    │
│                                                        │
│  User clicks button or changes input                   │
│  HTMX intercepts event (hx-post, hx-trigger="click")   │
│  Serializes all form inputs via `hx-include="#pdu-root"`│
└──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                           │ HTTP POST /_pdu/event/{State}/{method}
                           │ Body: application/x-www-form-urlencoded / JSON
                           ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   pyrustapi Server Core                │
│                                                        │
│  1. Restores Session from Cookie (`pdu-session`)       │
│  2. Deserializes form fields into State variables      │
│  3. Invokes state method: `State.method(**kwargs)`     │
│  4. Re-renders page fragment: `render_fragment()`      │
│  5. Returns HTML with updated state values (200 OK)    │
└──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                           │ HTTP 200 OK (HTML fragment)
                           ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      Client Browser                    │
│                                                        │
│  HTMX swaps `#pdu-root` innerHTML with new HTML       │
│  Tailwind applies updated styles instantaneously       │
│  DOM reflects mutated State without full page reload   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 2. Framework vs. Usage Diagnostic Matrix
docs.text: Symptom Layer Root Cause Resolution DevTools Console: TypeError: Cannot read property of undefined in htmx.min.js Framework Selector missing or invalid target (e.g. closest form when not in <form>). Fixed in v0.2.0: Unified hx-include="#pdu-root". Network Tab: 404 on /_pdu/static/htmx.min.js or .css Framework Static route handler only handling root files or missing MIME type. Fixed in v0.2.0: Streaming response with 18 MIME types and subfolder routing. Black transparent overlay blocks clicks to inputs/buttons Framework Backdrop z-index stacking above modal dialog card. Fixed in v0.2.0: Backdrop at z-index: 1, content strictly at z-index: 10. Server prints HTTP 500 without application traceback Framework Method invocation or page render lacked error boundaries. Fixed in v0.2.0: Error boundaries return #pdu-action-error toast instead of 500. Clicking button does not send any network request Usage Button lacks on_click or called method with parentheses: on_click=State.save() instead of on_click=State.save. Pass method reference: on_click=State.save. Form values are not saved / input value is empty on submit Usage Input missing bind or name: <input> without name cannot be serialized by HTML/HTMX. Add bind=State.my_var or name="my_var". State updates on server but UI displays old data Usage Referenced variable directly my_var instead of State class reference State.my_var. Use Heading(State.count) instead of reading inst.count. Changes not reflected after code edits Usage Running from different Python environment with old PyDataUI package. Ensure pip install -e . is installed in your active Python env.

docs.title: 3. Framework-Level Guarantees (PyDataUI v0.2.0)
docs.text:
1. Zero Client-Side JavaScript Required: Data developers never write JavaScript. All interactivity is declaratively compiled to HTMX attributes.

  2. Self-Healing Error Boundaries: If an exception occurs in your state method (e.g., database connection failure, validation error):

  3. The server never crashes with HTTP 500.
  4. Full traceback is logged to your terminal console.

  5. The UI remains interactive and displays an alert toast banner (#pdu-action-error) on the screen.

  6. Safe Multi-Environment Static Asset Serving: Static assets (htmx.min.js, pydataui.css, SVGs, fonts) are served with StreamingResponse to prevent Rust string-escaping and include CDN fallback onerror handlers.

  7. Descriptor & Falsy Binding Safety: bind=State.field safely retains the descriptor binding even when initial state values are empty strings "", 0, or False.

docs.title: ✅ Rule 1: Always Pass Method References (No Parentheses)
docs.text:
# ❌ INCORRECT (Executes during page render!):
Button("Save", on_click=MyState.save())

# ✅ CORRECT (Passes EventHandler descriptor to HTMX):
Button("Save", on_click=MyState.save)

docs.title: ✅ Rule 2: Pass Parameters Using with_args() or Lambdas
docs.text:
# Option A: with_args
Button("Edit", on_click=MyState.edit_item.with_args(item_id="123"))

# Option B: lambda with default argument
Button("Delete", on_click=lambda id=item.id: MyState.delete_item(id))

docs.title: ✅ Rule 3: Always Provide bind or name on Form Inputs
docs.text:
# ❌ INCORRECT (Will not serialize into request body!):
Input("Your Name")

# ✅ CORRECT (Automatically sets name="user_name" and binds state):
Input("Your Name", bind=MyState.user_name)

# ✅ ALSO CORRECT:
Input("Your Name", name="user_name")

docs.title: ✅ Rule 4: Use Accessible Modals and Dialogs
docs.text:
Modal(
    title="Create Entry",
    is_open=MyState.show_modal,
    on_close=MyState.close_modal,
    children=[
        Input("Title", bind=MyState.title),
        Button("Save", on_click=MyState.save),
    ]
)
Overlay backdrops automatically capture outside clicks to trigger on_close, while inputs inside the dialog card are fully interactive.
